name: Kýpros
rationale: No strong near-term BiCRS pathway here: municipal waste is the only significant feedstock but there is no waste-to-energy plant within range to retrofit with capture (and MSW is landfilled, not a removal feedstock), while other biomass — agricultural and forestry residues, manure — is limited. The options below are marginal at best.
caveats: Transport to the nearest storage project exceeds $100/tCO₂ for this pathway's payload — defaulted to a storage-independent option or densified bio-oil.

Mediterranean wildfire fuel management (shrub clearing, fuel breaks, thinning) generates woody residue, mostly left, mulched or burned today, but no open treated-area or biomass data exist here, so it is not quantified (Portugal is modelled from AGIF in the Europe scope).

Hydrothermal liquefaction densifies the carbon into a stable bio-crude, cheap to haul to distant wells
Viable where wet-slurry injection/AD would need nearby geologic storage
cons: Net of counterfactual debits: 50% gross − 9 pts soil carbon the spread manure would have built (50-yr) − 6 pts replacement fertilizer
Higher cost and earlier-stage than pyrolysis or direct injection
Lower CDR efficiency than slurry injection (~50% vs >90%)

ranked.label: AD RNG + CCS (upgrading CO₂)
pros: Manure is already digested here — AD+CCS retrofits existing biogas plants
Captures the near-pure CO2 already vented by biogas upgrading — cheap capture
RNG co-product displaces fossil gas; retrofits an existing biomethane plant
Digestate returns nutrients to fields
cons: Low CDR efficiency (~18% of manure carbon): the RNG carbon is combusted downstream (avoidance, not CDR)
Methane slip from digestion/upgrading erodes the removal (~12% of captured CO2 per 1% CH4 lost)
Transport to the nearest operating well is costly (~$85/tCO₂)
Geologic storage only moderately accessible — transport adds cost

ranked.label: AD + CCS (all carbon) + digestate injection
pros: Manure is already digested here — AD+CCS retrofits existing biogas plants

Energy co-product (electricity/heat); retrofits an existing CHP digester
cons: Net of counterfactual debits: 90% gross − 7 pts soil carbon the spread digestate would have built (50-yr) − 8 pts replacement fertilizer
One transport leg (CO₂ to its store, or digestate to the injection site) exceeds the $100/tCO₂ viability cap, so this pathway is not viable here
Digestate is mostly water — costly to haul to an injection site
Dilute flue-gas (or fuel-cell) capture at small plant scale is costly

name: Southern Scotland

storage_detail.nearest_project: Liverpool Bay CCS / HyNet T&S (Eni, Irish Sea)

rationale: Diffuse wet animal manure / biosolids, moderate nutrient status, good (low-cost) geologic storage access (~$13/tCO₂ delivered over ~432 km to Northern Endurance Partnership / Endurance (East Coast Cluster, UK)) -> wet feedstock far from affordable geologic storage favors hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) to a stable bio-crude (~35% CDR efficiency): it handles the wet biomass without drying and densifies the carbon for haulage to a distant well. Pricier than direct injection, so used only where storage is distant.
caveats: Bio-oil / biomass injection here would use Preesall salt caverns (Lancashire) — a prospective salt-cavern store, NOT yet developed or permitted for bio-oil/biomass storage in the UK. Treat as developable potential, not shovel-ready.
Transport to the nearest storage project exceeds $100/tCO₂ for this pathway's payload — defaulted to a storage-independent option or densified bio-oil.

name: Northern Ireland

storage_detail.nearest_project: Liverpool Bay CCS / HyNet T&S (Eni, Irish Sea)

rationale: Diffuse wet animal manure / biosolids, moderate nutrient status, good (low-cost) geologic storage access (~$53/tCO₂ delivered over ~359 km to Liverpool Bay CCS / HyNet T&S (Eni, Irish Sea)) -> wet wastes are unsuited to combustion (thesis sec 2.2); Vaulted-style slurry injection delivers ~75% net CDR efficiency (after the forgone-soil-carbon and fertilizer-replacement debits) with PFAS-destruction co-benefit.
